newsitem.title: USA: Senate funds probe opens with surprises.
newsitem.headline: Senate funds probe opens with surprises.

text.p: A Senate probe into political fund-raising scandals opened on Tuesday with a dramatic allegation by its Republican chairman that China contrived to buy its way into American politics.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee also received a surprise offer of testimony by a key player in the tangled web of donations, John Huang. His lawyer said Huang agreed to speak "truthfully to the best of his knowledge and honest recollection," if given limited immunity from prosecution.

Committee chairman Fred Thompson of Tennessee, who sharpened his prosecutorial skills as Republican counsel during the Senate Watergate hearings, promised non-partisan and wide-ranging hearings to search for truth about foreign influence in the 1996 presidential race as well as alleged violations of campaign financing laws.
"The chase for money to seek public office has led most of us to push the envelope ... to push the law to the limit," Democratic Sen. Carl Levin of Michigan said.
The 1996 congressional and presidential campaigns broke all records with more than $600 million spent, nearly 50 percent higher than the 1991-92 cycle.

Thompson began the long-awaited televised hearings with a statement that Beijing's communist leaders had a plan to build political influence in the United States, a charge China has denied. "The committee believes that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process," he said.

Apart from foreign influence the panel over the next four weeks will examine reports of sleepovers in the White House Lincoln Bedroom for campaign high-rollers, alleged calls to solicit funds made from the White House by Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, and Gore's attendance at a fund raiser in a Buddhist temple with monks who have taken a vow of poverty.

Clinton, whose popularity has remained high despite the seemingly endless stream of revelations on the fund-raising controversy, declined comment. At a Madrid meeting on NATO expansion, he attempted to brush aside the question. "I can't comment on it," Clinton said. "I've been working here."

Thompson had no immediate response to Huang's offer to appear, which was transmitted at 8:47 a.m. EDT in a letter by his lawyer, Ty Cobb, to Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the panel's senior Democrat. Cobb said the limited immunity would not protect Huang from charges of economic espionage, disclosure of classified information or perjury.
A Justice Department official said it was too early to say whether the offer would acceptable.

Huang is a former Commerce Department official who became a top fundraiser for the Democratic National Committee. The DNC returned $1.6 million raised by him from questionable sources and before Tuesday he had cited his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in refusing to testify.
Former senior White House and Democratic party aides are among the potential first witnesses to be called on Wednesday but two other key figures have fled the country.

Charles Yah Lin Trie, a former Arkansas restauranteur and Clinton friend who became a major Democratic fundraiser, was believed to be in Shanghai. He raised or donated $645,000 the DNC later returned. Pauline Kanchanalak, whose $560,000 donation to the Democrats is being investigated, was thought to be in Thailand.

Among key witnesses subpoenaed to appear are four aides close to Clinton and the Democratic party: Harold Ickes, formerly Clinton's deputy chief of staff, Don Fowler, former Democratic National Committee co-chairman, long-time Clinton confidant Bruce Lindsey and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's former chief of staff Maggie Williams.

Concerning China's actions in the 1996 campaign, Thompson said the plan to gain political influence in the United States was drawn up to respond to advances by Taiwan in building influence in Washington and included "typical appropriate" measures such as hiring lobbyists and diplomatic visits.

But he said Beijing had shown an interest in "developing long-term relationships with persons it has identified as up-and-coming officials at state and local levels. The intent is to establish relations that can be cultivated as the officials rise through the ranks to higher office."

Glenn warned against a "jump to conclusions," asking: "Is there any real evidence that the Chinese government, or any other foreign government, actually infiltrated the American government via campaign contributions?"
